whyNot.1: Sodium fluoride inhibits glycolysis; it plays no role in preserving bilirubin.
whyNot.2: Light exposure photo-oxidizes bilirubin and gives falsely low results.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Amniotic Fluid (specimen handling and processing).

items.stem: During a urine collection for workplace drug testing, the collector must check the specimen temperature to detect substitution. When must the temperature be read, and what range is acceptable?
items.why: Freshly voided urine is near body temperature but cools quickly. **The temperature must be read within 4 minutes of collection and should be about 32 to 38 °C (90 to 100 °F).** A reading outside this range suggests a substituted or adulterated specimen; it is recorded, and a new collection is usually required.

whyNot.0: After an hour the urine has cooled to room temperature, so the reading could no longer show that it came from the donor.
whyNot.2: A specimen this cool within 4 minutes is below the expected body-temperature range and suggests substitution.
whyNot.3: Waiting 30 minutes allows the urine to cool, and a range up to 40 °C is above normal body temperature.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Introduction to Urinalysis (drug specimen collection).

items.stem: A technologist wants to view urine sediment elements with a three-dimensional, relief-like appearance and without a halo artifact. Which type of microscopy provides this?
items.why: Interference-contrast systems split the light beam and recombine it after it passes through the specimen. **Interference-contrast microscopy (such as Nomarski differential interference contrast) produces a three-dimensional image** with fine detail and without the halo seen in phase contrast.

whyNot.1: Phase contrast improves visibility of low-refractive elements such as hyaline casts, but it surrounds objects with a halo of light.
whyNot.2: Darkfield shows bright objects on a dark background and is used for organisms such as Treponema pallidum.
whyNot.3: Polarized light identifies birefringent crystals, cholesterol, and fibers; it does not give a three-dimensional image.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Microscopic Examination of Urine (types of microscopy).

items.stem: A urinalysis procedure requires centrifugation at a relative centrifugal force (RCF) of 400 × g. The centrifuge rotor has a radius of 15 cm. At about what speed should the centrifuge be set? (RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × radius in cm × rpm²)
items.why: Rearrange the formula: rpm = √(RCF ÷ (1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r)) = √(400 ÷ (1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 15)) = √2,385,000 ≈ 1,540 rpm. **RCF depends on the rotor radius and the square of the speed**, so the same rpm gives different forces in centrifuges of different sizes.

whyNot.0: This uses the radius in millimeters (150) instead of centimeters.
whyNot.1: This uses the rotor diameter (30 cm) instead of the radius.
whyNot.3: This uses half the radius (7.5 cm), which overestimates the speed needed.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Microscopic Examination of Urine (specimen preparation; centrifugation).

worked.problem: A centrifuge with a 12-cm rotor radius runs at 2,000 rpm. What RCF does it produce?
steps: RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × rpm².

items.stem: A patient with ethanol intoxication has a serum osmolality of 360 mOsm/kg by freezing point depression but only 300 mOsm/kg on a vapor pressure osmometer. What explains the difference?
options: Freezing point osmometers do not detect ethanol
Vapor pressure osmometers do not detect volatile solutes
Ethanol elevates the serum freezing point
Unseparated serum produced lactic acid during storage
items.why: Volatile solutes such as ethanol and methanol evaporate along with water, so they do not lower the measured vapor pressure. **Vapor pressure osmometers miss volatile solutes, whereas freezing point osmometers detect them**, which is why freezing point depression is used when an osmolal gap from alcohol is suspected.

whyNot.0: The opposite is true: freezing point depression counts the ethanol, which is why that result is higher.
whyNot.2: Like any solute, ethanol lowers the freezing point; it does not raise it.
whyNot.3: Lactic acid formed in an unseparated specimen would raise the result on both instruments, not only on the freezing point method.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Renal Function (osmolality; freezing point and vapor pressure osmometers).

items.stem: A large volume of a corrosive reagent spills down the front of a technologist's lab coat and soaks through to the skin of her chest and arm. What should she do first?
options: Keep the coat on and rinse only the exposed skin of her arm at the sink
Get under the safety shower, remove the contaminated clothing, and flush for at least 15 minutes
Wipe the skin with alcohol to dissolve the reagent before rinsing
Finish containing the spill, then go to the supervisor for first aid
items.why: Chemical contact with the skin must be diluted and removed at once to limit tissue damage. **For a large splash, use the safety shower, remove contaminated clothing, and flush the skin with running water for at least 15 minutes**, then seek medical attention and report the incident.

whyNot.0: Soaked clothing holds the chemical against the skin, so it must come off, and a large area needs the safety shower rather than a sink.
whyNot.2: Alcohol does not safely remove a corrosive and only delays flushing; water comes first.
whyNot.3: Spill cleanup and reporting come after first aid; any delay lets the chemical keep burning.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Safety and Quality Management (chemical hazards).

items.stem: A laboratory's urinalysis controls are always within limits, yet the director also enrolls the laboratory in proficiency testing. What does proficiency testing evaluate that daily internal quality control cannot?
options: Whether patient specimens were collected and labeled correctly
Whether the laboratory's results on unknown samples agree with those of other laboratories
Whether the method's day-to-day precision is acceptable
Whether a new reagent strip lot performs like the previous lot
items.why: Internal quality control uses the laboratory's own controls with known values and shows that a method is stable from run to run. **Proficiency testing sends unknown samples from an outside agency and grades each laboratory's results against its peers, an external check on accuracy** that accrediting and licensing bodies require.

whyNot.0: Collection and labeling are pre-examination steps checked by specimen acceptance and rejection criteria, not by proficiency testing.
whyNot.2: Day-to-day precision is what the laboratory's own internal control charts monitor.
whyNot.3: A new lot is checked by running the laboratory's own controls on it before use.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Safety and Quality Management (external quality control).

items.stem: A urine hCG cassette shows a colored line in the control region in addition to the test result. What does the appearance of this built-in control line verify?
options: That the patient's hCG is within the measurable range
That enough specimen was added and the reagents migrated and reacted
That the lot of cassettes agrees with other laboratories' results
That external liquid controls no longer need to be run
items.why: Built-in (procedural) controls are a form of internal quality control. **The control line confirms that adequate specimen was applied, the fluid migrated properly, and the reagents were active**; it does not verify the accuracy of the patient result at specific concentrations. External positive and negative liquid controls are still run as the laboratory and manufacturer require.

whyNot.0: The control line forms regardless of the hCG level; it says nothing about the analyte concentration.
whyNot.2: Comparison with other laboratories is the purpose of proficiency testing, not of a built-in control line.
whyNot.3: Built-in controls do not replace external liquid controls, which are still required at set intervals and with new lots or shipments.

items.ref: Strasinger SK, Di Lorenzo MS. Urinalysis and Body Fluids, 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2021, chapter on Safety and Quality Management (internal quality control).
